lesson.title: The Blink Before Memory: Sensory Memory
lesson.summary: Sensory memory is the first and briefest stage of the multi-store model, holding a rich but rapidly fading trace of a stimulus just long enough for attention to select what gets processed further.
lesson.body:
Sensory memory is the first and briefest of the three stores in the multi-store memory model, holding an extremely short-lived, high-capacity trace of incoming sensory information immediately after a stimulus is detected. Psychologists generally distinguish two types tied to different senses. Iconic memory holds visual information for a fraction of a second, typically well under a second, while echoic memory holds auditory information a bit longer, for a few seconds. In both cases, sensory memory functions like a very brief buffer, preserving a rich, near-complete snapshot of what the senses just took in for just long enough that attention has a chance to select which parts deserve further processing.

What sensory memory can register is limited by the same absolute threshold that governs sensation more broadly, the minimum stimulus intensity needed for detection to occur at all. Sensory memory is not a record of the full physical stimulus in the environment; it is a record of whatever portion of that stimulus actually crossed the threshold and registered as a sensation in the first place. A sound too quiet to be heard, or a flash too dim to be seen, never makes it into sensory memory, since there was no detected sensation there to hold onto.

One of the clearest classic demonstrations of iconic memory's large capacity and rapid fading comes from research using what is known as the partial report technique. Participants briefly viewed a grid of letters flashed for a fraction of a second and were then asked to report as many letters as they could. When asked to report the entire grid, people could typically recall only a handful of letters. But when cued, immediately after the flash, to report just one specific row of the grid, people could report that row almost perfectly, regardless of which row was cued, suggesting that far more of the grid had briefly been available in sensory memory than a full report could capture before it faded. This pattern showed that iconic memory holds a surprisingly complete image for a moment, even though most of it decays before it can be consciously reported.

Sensory memory is the entry point for the entire multi-store pipeline. If attention is directed toward some portion of the information sitting briefly in sensory memory, that portion gets passed along into short-term memory for further processing. If attention is not directed toward it in time, the trace simply decays and is lost permanently, never having reached any more durable store. This is why sensory memory, despite briefly holding so much information, contributes so little to what people consciously remember: only the sliver that attention manages to select in time survives the transition to the next stage.

Sensory memory shows up in a few familiar everyday experiences. Waving a lit sparkler or a flashlight quickly through the dark seems to leave a glowing trail behind it, an illusion created because iconic memory briefly retains the after-image of each earlier position even as the light moves on. Echoic memory shows up when someone asks "what did you just say" right after you were not fully listening, and you find yourself able to mentally replay the last second or two of sound well enough to answer, because the echoic trace of that sound was still lingering in sensory memory even though attention had not been focused on it at the time.
